senses.definition: To acknowledge a dancing partner by facing them and moving first to one side and then to the other, while they do the opposite.
senses.example: Set to partners! was the next instruction from the caller.

senses.definition: To place or fix in a setting.
senses.example: to set a precious stone in a border of metal

senses.definition: To put in order in a particular manner; to prepare.
senses.example: to set (that is, to hone) a razor

senses.definition: To extend and bring into position; to spread.
senses.example: to set the sails of a ship

senses.definition: To give a pitch to, as a tune; to start by fixing the keynote.
senses.example: The choir director set the pitch with a tuning fork before the first verse.

senses.definition: To reduce from a dislocated or fractured state.
senses.example: to set a broken bone

senses.definition: To lower into place and fix solidly, as the blocks of cut stone in a structure.
senses.example: Masons set each granite block carefully, using mortar to hold it in place.

senses.definition: To adorn with something infixed or affixed; to stud; to variegate with objects placed here and there.
senses.example: The velvet case was set with tiny diamonds that glittered under the lamp.

senses.definition: To establish as a rule; to furnish; to prescribe; to assign.
senses.example: to set a good example

senses.definition: To cause (a domestic fowl) to sit on eggs to brood.
senses.example: To set a hen.

senses.definition: To arrange the casting of a movie.
senses.example: Paramount Pictures has set Jennifer Love Hewitt for a movie called Two Can Play This Game.

senses.definition: To produce after pollination.
senses.example: to set seed

senses.definition: (dated) To cause to stop or stick; to obstruct; to fasten to a spot.
senses.example: to set a coach in the mud
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: A punch for setting nails in wood.
senses.example: nail set

senses.definition: A device for receiving broadcast radio waves (or, more recently, broadcast data); a radio or television.
senses.example: television set

senses.definition: A small tuber or bulb used instead of seed, particularly onion sets and potato sets.
The amount by which the teeth of a saw protrude to the side in order to create the kerf.
A permanent change of shape caused by excessive strain, as from compression, tension, bending, twisting, etc.
senses.example: the set of a spring

senses.definition: A bias of mind; an attitude or pattern of behavior.
A piece placed temporarily upon the head of a pile when the latter cannot otherwise be reached by the weight, or hammer.
A young oyster when first attached.
Collectively, the crop of young oysters in any locality.
A series or group of something. (Note the similar meaning in Etymology 4, Noun)
The manner, state, or quality of setting or fitting; fit.
senses.example: the set of a coat

senses.definition: The pattern of a tartan, etc.
The camber of a curved roofing tile.
The full number of eggs set under a hen.
A tool for dressing forged iron.
A young plant fit for setting out; a slip; shoot.
A rudimentary fruit.
The setting of the sun or other luminary; the close of the day.
General movement; direction; drift; tendency.
A matching collection of similar things. (Note the similar meaning in Etymology 2, Noun.)
senses.example: a set of tables

senses.definition: A collection of various objects for a particular purpose.
senses.example: a set of tools

senses.definition: An object made up of several parts.
senses.example: a set of steps

senses.definition: A collection of zero or more objects, possibly infinite in size, and disregarding any order or repetition of the objects which may be contained within it.
Set theory.
A group of people, usually meeting socially or connected through some shared interest, activity, attribute, etc.
senses.example: the country set

senses.definition: The scenery for a film or play.

The general locations and area where a movie’s, a film’s, or a video’s scenery is arranged to be filmed also including places for actors, assorted crew, director, producers which are typically not filmed.
The initial or basic formation of dancers.
A group of repetitions of a single exercise performed one after the other without rest.
A complete series of games, forming part of a match.
A complete series of points, forming part of a match.
The act of directing the ball to a teammate for an attack.
Three of a kind, especially if two cards are in one's hand and the third is on the board. Compare trips (“three of a kind, especially with two cards on the board and one in one's hand”).
A musical performance by a band, disc jockey, etc. consisting of several musical pieces.
A drum kit, a drum set.
senses.example: He plays the set on Saturdays.

senses.definition: (dated) The width of the body of a type.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Fixed in position.
Rigid, solidified.
Ready, prepared.
senses.example: on your marks, get set, go!; on your marks, set, go!

senses.definition: Intent, determined (to do something).
senses.example: set on getting to his destination

senses.definition: Prearranged.
senses.example: a set menu

senses.definition: Fixed in one’s opinion.
senses.example: I’m set against the idea of smacking children to punish them.

senses.definition: Fixed in a certain style.

core.definition: To put or place something somewhere, usually carefully and in a particular position or state.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short e, as in bed, and release the final t crisply. Do not make the vowel long or confuse it with sit, which has a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a very ordinary, everyday verb that carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Set is one of the most common verbs in American English, used for placing objects, adjusting devices, setting goals, and forming many phrasal verbs. The exact meaning depends on the object, so set the table, set the alarm, and set a goal all mean different things. Native speakers use it constantly in home, work and everyday life.

distinctions.note: Put is the general word for placing something, while set often implies deliberate, precise placement or adjustment.
Sit is intransitive and takes no object, while set is transitive and needs an object, as in set the cup down, not sit the cup down.
Lay is transitive and means to put something down, while lie is intransitive and means to rest; many Americans confuse lay and lie.

examples.everyday: Could you set the table while I finish the salad?
examples.professional: Let's set a deadline for the model review before the next sprint starts.
examples.analytical: The essay sets two definitions of justice side by side so that the reader can weigh their merits.

nuance.analogy: Like placing a book on a shelf: you decide exactly where it stays.
nuance.etymology: From Old English settan, to cause to sit, related to sit.
common_mistakes: Using set without an object, as in The sun is setting is fine, but I set in the chair is wrong; use sat.
Confusing set and sit, especially with the past tense set and sat.

set.etymology: From Middle English *setten*, from Old English *settan*, from **sattjan*, from Proto-Germanic **satjaną*, from Proto-Indo-European **sodéyeti*, causative of **sed-* (“to sit”).

senses.definition: To put into an angry mood; to start (a person) ranting or sulking, etc.
senses.example: Don't set him off or he won't shut up all day.

senses.definition: To leave; to set out; to begin a journey or trip.
senses.example: He set off in search of better opportunities.

senses.definition: To begin; to cause; to initiate.
senses.example: I had no idea that one simple comment would set off such a huge argument.

senses.definition: To cause to begin.
senses.example: When he started giggling, it set us all off too.

senses.definition: To cause to explode, let off.
senses.example: What a tragedy, that someone would set off a bomb in a crowded place.

senses.definition: To enhance by emphasizing differences.
senses.example: Her plain white dress was set off by a bright red stole.

senses.definition: To offset, to compensate for: to reduce the effect of, by having a contrary effect.
senses.example: My taxes did not increase because the amount of my raise was set off by my losses in the stock market.

senses.definition: (historical) To deface or soil the next sheet; said of the ink on a freshly printed sheet, when another sheet comes in contact with it before it has had time to dry.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: To begin a journey or leave on a trip; also, to trigger something such as an alarm or an explosion.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'off', the second word, so say 'set AWF'. In fast speech the t of 'set' is often flapped or linked into 'off', sounding like 'seh-DOFF'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The leaving sense is ordinary, while the triggering sense can be neutral or mildly negative depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'set off' all the time for starting a trip, such as 'We set off at six.' It is less formal than 'set out', which sounds more planned. The same phrase also means triggering an alarm or causing an argument, so listen for context. A natural reply to 'When are you setting off?' is simply giving a time.

distinctions.note: Set out is slightly more formal and can mean starting a plan or intention, while set off is more common for leaving on a trip.
Leave is the general word for departing, while set off adds the sense of starting a journey or a process.
Trigger means causing a reaction, and it sounds more technical; set off is the everyday phrasal verb for the same effect with alarms or events.

examples.everyday: We should set off before traffic gets bad, so let's leave by seven.
examples.professional: The rollout set off a series of alerts, so we paused it and checked the logs.
examples.analytical: Mill's argument set off a long debate about liberty and harm that still shapes how philosophers frame public policy.

nuance.analogy: Setting off is like pulling the starting gun: the race begins, or the alarm goes off, once the trigger is pulled.
nuance.etymology: From Old English settan, to cause to sit or place, combined with Old English of, meaning away.
common_mistakes: Using 'set off' for leaving when 'set out' would be more natural in formal writing about plans.
Forgetting the preposition: say 'set off for' a place, as in 'set off for the airport'.

conversation.text: We set off for the mountains at six in the morning.
Burnt toast set off the smoke alarm again.
Anything can set him off when he's tired.
They set off early to beat the traffic.
My belt buckle set off the metal detector at security.

senses.definition: The quality of being sexual; that which is characterized or distinguished by sex.
Sexual activity; concern with, or interest in, sexual activity.
senses.example: The novel's frank treatment of sexuality shocked some early readers but drew praise from critics.

senses.definition: Sexual potency.
Sexual orientation.
Sexual identity, gender.

core.definition: A person's sexual orientation or identity, or the general quality of being sexual.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the al syllable, with the sh sound in the middle. In fast speech the t in the last syllable often becomes a soft flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but personal and sometimes sensitive. The meaning depends on whether the speaker is discussing biology, identity or a person's private life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sexuality in health, education and identity contexts, often to mean sexual orientation such as gay, straight or bisexual. People usually describe their own orientation rather than being asked, so avoid prying at work. In academic writing it can also refer to sexual nature in general.

distinctions.note: Sexual orientation is the specific term for who a person is attracted to; sexuality is broader and includes identity and sexual nature.
Gender identity is a person's internal sense of their gender; sexuality concerns attraction and sexual nature, and the two are different.

examples.everyday: My sister is figuring out her sexuality, and she just wants us to listen.
examples.professional: Our health curriculum includes a unit on human sexuality, so teachers must follow the district guidelines.
examples.analytical: In her book, she argues that sexuality cannot be reduced to desire, because it shapes identity, power and social belonging.

nuance.analogy: Like a color running through a painting, sexuality shapes many parts of who a person is.
nuance.etymology: From sexual, from Latin sexus, sex, with the suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Using sexuality to mean only sexual activity; it is broader and covers identity and orientation.
Stressing the first syllable or the -ity ending, instead of the al syllable.

senses.definition: In a shaky manner.

core.definition: In a trembling, unsteady way, such as when someone's hands or voice shake from nerves, cold, or weakness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel is short, like 'ih', and the final -ly is 'lee'; do not add an extra syllable such as 'shake-ih-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on context, since it describes nervousness, weakness, or fragility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for a voice, hands, a stance, or handwriting: 'She stood up shakily and reached for the rail.' It is common in everyday storytelling and writing. Spoken, it often suggests someone recovering from a shock or illness, and it is not used for balance, where 'unsteadily' is better.

distinctions.note: Unsteadily describes balance and movement, such as walking on a boat or a wobbly ladder; shakily describes trembling from nerves, cold, or weakness.
Nervously focuses on the emotion behind an action; shakily focuses on the visible trembling.

examples.everyday: He got up shakily after the fall and said he was fine.
examples.professional: She described the outage shakily on the call, so I asked her to walk us through the timeline again.
examples.analytical: The author writes shakily about the doctrine of grace, as if the argument has not yet found its footing.

nuance.analogy: Like a glass of water on a moving train: the surface wobbles with each jolt, and the wobble reveals the motion underneath.
nuance.etymology: Formed from shaky and the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'shakingly' in everyday speech; the usual adverb is 'shakily'.
Confusing shakily (trembling) with unsteadily (losing balance).

senses.definition: To shine tremulously or intermittently; to gleam faintly.
senses.example: Sunlight began to shimmer across the lake as the wind settled.

senses.definition: Of a mass of bees: to move their abdomens in a coordinated manner so as to produce a shimmering wave effect, thought to deter predators.
senses.example: Scientists watched the bees shimmer on the comb as the hive faced a threat.

senses.definition: A faint or veiled and tremulous gleam or shining.
senses.example: A faint shimmer of light appeared on the water just before dawn.

senses.definition: A measure of the irregularities in the loudness of a particular pitch over time.
senses.example: The engineer measured the shimmer of the tone to check the instrument's stability.

senses.definition: A thin electronic device that is fit inside a card reader, such as on automated teller machines (ATMs), or point-of-sale terminals (POS's), that acts as an intermediate interface between the chip on a chip-and-pin technology card and the chip reader of the machine, to allow one to clone the chip.
senses.example: Police found a shimmer hidden inside the gas pump's card reader last Tuesday.

core.definition: To shine with a faint, trembling light that seems to flicker or shift, such as sunlight on water or heat in the air.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -er is an American r-colored vowel, so pronounce the r clearly and do not say 'shimma.' Keep the mm as one held sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests beauty and softness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shimmer for light on water, silk, heat haze, or makeup, as in 'shimmer eyeshadow.' It is common in everyday speech and also in writing and advertising. It describes a soft, moving light, so do not use it for a bright, sudden flash.

distinctions.note: Glimmer is fainter and often briefer, while shimmer implies a steadier, trembling quality.
Sparkle means many small bright flashes, while shimmer is softer and more even.
Glitter is brighter and more showy, often from many reflecting points.

examples.everyday: The lake shimmered in the late afternoon sun, and we just sat on the dock watching it.
examples.professional: The new dashboard uses a subtle shimmer on the active tab, so it stands out without distracting users.
examples.analytical: Heat haze makes distant objects shimmer, so their outlines seem to tremble as the air moves.

nuance.analogy: Like sunlight wobbling on a pool when the water is stirred gently.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English shimeren, of Germanic origin; the exact root is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using shimmer for a bright, sudden flash; it means a soft, trembling light
Pronouncing the final -er as a full separate syllable, as in 'shim-mer-ah'

shimmer.etymology: From Middle English *schimeren*, from Old English *sċymrian*, *sċimrian*, *sċimerian*, from Proto-Germanic **skimarōną*.

senses.definition: A load of goods that is transported by any method (not just by ship).
senses.example: We're expecting another shipment of oranges tomorrow.

senses.definition: The act of transporting goods.
senses.example: Shipment of hazardous waste on this route is strictly prohibited.

core.definition: A quantity of goods sent together from one place to another, usually by a single transport method.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ment is a weak, reduced syllable that sounds like 'mint' without a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, business word with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shipment in business, logistics, retail, and everyday conversation about packages. It refers to a batch of goods being sent, not the process of sending. For the arrival of a package to a customer, Americans often say delivery.

distinctions.note: Shipment is the goods being sent; delivery is the act of bringing them to the recipient.
Consignment is a more formal or technical word for a shipment sent to an agent or buyer, often used in trade contracts.
Freight is the goods carried by a transport system or the cost of carrying them, not the batch itself.

examples.everyday: My order is a day late, but the tracking says the shipment left the warehouse this morning.
examples.professional: The second shipment of server parts is delayed until Thursday, so we need a temporary fix.
examples.analytical: Each shipment in the supply chain carries risk, and a good contract assigns that risk explicitly.

nuance.analogy: A shipment is like one moving truck loaded with everything from one household: many items, one trip.
nuance.etymology: From ship (verb) plus the suffix -ment, meaning the result or act of shipping.
common_mistakes: Making it plural wrongly in counting: 'I received three shipment' should be 'three shipments.'
Confusing shipment with delivery: a shipment is the goods, while the delivery is their arrival.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of keyboard shortcut.
A path between two points that is faster than the commonly used paths.
senses.example: We took a shortcut through the park to reach the station before the train left.

senses.definition: A method to accomplish something that omits one or more steps.
senses.example: Learning the keyboard shortcut for copy and paste saved me hours of clicking.

senses.definition: A file that points to the location of another file and serves as a quick way to access it.
senses.example: There are shortcuts to some of my favorite applications on my desktop.

senses.definition: To take or use a shortcut.
senses.example: Don't shortcut the safety checks just because the deadline is tomorrow morning.

core.definition: A faster route between two places, or a quick method that skips some steps.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'SHORT,' and the vowel is the 'aw' of 'short,' not the 'oh' sound. The final 'cut' has a short u and a crisp t, with no extra vowel after the t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it means a useful time-saver, but negative when it implies skipping important steps.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'take a shortcut' for a faster route, and 'shortcut' for a method that saves time. In professional talk, 'shortcuts' can imply cutting corners, so a careful speaker adds details. On computers, 'keyboard shortcut' is the common phrase for a key combination.

distinctions.note: A detour is a longer alternate route around a blocked path; a shortcut is a faster path.
A hack is a clever trick, often informal; a shortcut is a simpler way that may skip steps.

examples.everyday: Let's take the shortcut through the park so we're not stuck in traffic.
examples.professional: Using the keyboard shortcut for copying saves a few minutes on every report.
examples.analytical: A shortcut in reasoning, such as assuming correlation implies causation, can make an argument look convincing while skipping essential steps.

nuance.analogy: Like a footpath worn across a grassy field, cutting the corner of the long route.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'short' and 'cut.'
common_mistakes: Writing 'short cut' as two words in formal writing, which is acceptable but less common now.
Saying 'do a shortcut' instead of 'take a shortcut.'

conversation.text: I know a shortcut through the back streets.
The shortcut took longer because of a train crossing.
Use the keyboard shortcut to copy and paste.

senses.definition: Muscular power, muscle; nerve, nervous energy; vigor, vigorous strength.
senses.example: The old wrestler still had the sinew to lift the heavy bag above his head.

senses.definition: That which gives strength or in which strength consists; a supporting factor or member; mainstay.
senses.example: Her faith was the sinew that carried the family through years of hardship.

senses.definition: A cord or tendon of the body.
senses.example: The surgeon carefully repaired the torn sinew in his injured ankle.

senses.definition: A cord or string, particularly as of a musical instrument.
senses.example: She tightened the sinew of the old harp before the concert began.

senses.definition: To knit together or make strong with, or as if with, sinews.
senses.example: Years of disciplined training sinewed his arms and shoulders into hard, lean strength.

core.definition: Tough fibrous tissue that connects muscle to bone; a tendon. Also, strength or the thing that provides it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is 'yoo', so the word sounds like 'SIN-yoo', not 'sin-EW'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in anatomy; positive when used figuratively for strength, endurance, or the core of something.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech, sinew is mostly found in literary, descriptive, or sports writing, and it usually refers to strong, visible tendons or to toughness. People say 'tendon' or 'muscle' in medical or everyday talk. Figurative use, such as 'the sinews of war' or 'the sinew of the economy,' sounds formal but natural.

distinctions.note: A tendon is the precise anatomical term for tissue joining muscle to bone, while sinew is older, more general, and often used figuratively for strength.
A ligament connects bone to bone, while sinew usually refers to tissue connecting muscle to bone.

examples.everyday: He's all sinew and no fat, which is why he runs so fast.
examples.professional: The team's sinew is its senior engineers, who hold the system together when deadlines slip.
examples.analytical: Scripture describes the human body as knit together with bones and sinews, a picture of created frailty and dependence.

nuance.analogy: Sinew is the rope that connects the engine to the wheels: without it, the power never reaches the ground.
nuance.etymology: From Old English seonu, related to Germanic words for tendon and sinew.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'SIN-yoo-ee' with an extra syllable instead of two syllables.
Confusing it with 'sinuous', which means winding or curving.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word gid (sinew, tendon) appears in Genesis 32:32, where the sinew of the hip is connected with Jacob's wrestling. In Job 10:11 the speaker describes God knitting him together with bones and sinews, showing the body as made and sustained by God. Both passages present sinew as a sign of the body's created structure and its dependence on God.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being sinless.

core.definition: The state of never having sinned, or of being free from sin, in a moral or religious sense.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The -less and -ness endings are reduced, so both sound like short uh-s sounds, with no stress.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It names an ideal state, and in debates it can be discussed critically.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sinlessness mainly in theology, church discussion, and literary writing; in everyday speech people say perfection or innocence. Using it casually can sound preachy. In academic debates it often refers to whether Christ or Mary possessed it.

distinctions.note: Innocence also means not guilty of a crime, while sinlessness is specifically about moral or religious perfection.
Holiness means being set apart for God and includes positive character, while sinlessness stresses the absence of sin.
Impeccability is a technical theological term for being unable to sin, while sinlessness describes not having sinned.

examples.everyday: I don't claim sinlessness, but I'm trying to do better every day.
examples.professional: In the seminar, the speaker questioned whether sinlessness is a realistic goal for members of a congregation.
examples.analytical: The argument for the sinlessness of Christ depends on distinguishing a human nature from the will to sin, a distinction that Hebrews 4:15 supports.

nuance.analogy: Like a clear lake untouched by runoff, sinlessness describes a life with nothing polluting it.
nuance.etymology: Formed from sinless and the suffix -ness; sin comes from Old English synn.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in sin-LESS-ness; the stress belongs on SIN.
Using it in legal contexts where innocence is the correct word.
nuance.biblical_note: Sinlessness in Scripture refers chiefly to Christ, who is described as having committed no sin and as tempted without yielding. The Greek word behind sin is hamartia, a missing of the mark. John 8:7 uses the Greek anamartētos, without sin, in a context about judgment. Hebrews 4:15 describes Jesus as tested in all things yet without sin, and 2 Corinthians 5:21 says he knew no sin.

traditions.view: Sinlessness is affirmed of Christ as true God and true man, and the Theotokos is honored as all-holy and free from personal sin, without a Catholic-style dogma of the Immaculate Conception.
Christ is sinless, and Mary was preserved from original sin by singular grace, defined as the Immaculate Conception in 1854, while ordinary believers remain sinners who can be sanctified.

Protestants affirm the sinlessness of Christ but generally deny a special exemption for Mary and deny that believers are sinless in this life; Wesleyan and Holiness Christians teach entire sanctification, while Reformed and Lutheran traditions stress simul iustus et peccator.

senses.definition: The property of being slick.
senses.example: The slickness of the wet pavement made the morning commute dangerous.

core.definition: The quality of being smooth, polished or slippery, often describing a surface or a highly polished presentation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is short and unstressed, and the final '-ness' is a short 'nis', not 'nace'.

nuance.connotation: Mixed. It can praise a smooth, professional presentation, but often suggests a polished surface that hides something, so it can sound slightly negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slickness for a polished pitch, a product's finish or a road's surface, especially when they want to suggest it is a little too smooth. For a sincere or elegant look, sleekness is more positive. In formal writing, use smoothness or polish for a neutral tone.

distinctions.note: Smoothness is neutral and literal; slickness can suggest a surface or manner that is smooth in a shallow or artificial way.
Sleekness is positive and suggests elegant, streamlined lines; slickness can imply too much polish or insincerity.
Polish is a generally positive word for skill and refinement; slickness can suggest that the polish is superficial.

examples.everyday: The video had a lot of slickness, but I still did not believe a word of the pitch.
examples.professional: The team admired the slickness of the vendor's demo, but they asked for the raw data behind it.
examples.analytical: The author's prose has a remarkable slickness that sometimes disguises the gaps in her reasoning.

nuance.analogy: Slickness is like a freshly painted house: it looks perfect from the street, but you still need to check the foundation.
nuance.etymology: From slick (Old English slician, to make smooth) plus the noun suffix -ness, meaning the quality of being.
common_mistakes: Confusing slickness with sleekness; slickness can suggest too much polish, while sleekness is usually positive.
Using slickness as a neutral word in a context where it sounds like criticism.

senses.definition: I forgot.

core.definition: I forgot something, or it went out of my memory without my noticing.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on "mind," and "my" is reduced to a quick sound. The final t of "slipped" is often flapped or dropped before the m, so it sounds like "slip-my."

nuance.connotation: Neutral to apologetic; it softens forgetting by suggesting it was accidental, so it is polite when apologizing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "it slipped my mind" to apologize for forgetting a task, a birthday, or a meeting. It is friendly and less blunt than "I forgot." A natural reply is "No worries" or "That's okay, it happens."

distinctions.note: "I forgot" is direct and neutral, while "it slipped my mind" sounds more apologetic and conversational.
"Spaced" is very casual slang and can sound careless, while "slipped my mind" is polite for most situations.

examples.everyday: Oh no, I'm sorry, I completely forgot to pick up milk. It just slipped my mind.
examples.professional: Sorry, the report slipped my mind this morning; I'll send it to you before noon.
examples.analytical: When a moral duty slips our mind, the failure may reveal less about our intentions than about our attention and habits.

nuance.analogy: Like a slippery fish that escapes your grasp, a memory can slip away before you hold onto it.
nuance.etymology: From slip (Middle English slippen) plus mind (Old English gemynd), memory or thought.
common_mistakes: Saying "it slipped out of my mind" in a mismatched context; both work, but "slipped my mind" is more common.
Pronouncing "slipped" as "slipt" with an unnatural separate t.

conversation.text: Sorry I didn't call. It completely slipped my mind.
The dentist appointment totally slipped my mind.
I meant to send you the file, but it slipped my mind.

senses.definition: Used in adjectival compounds.
senses.example: foul-smelling (having a foul smell)

senses.definition: The act by which something is smelled.
senses.example: The smelling of fresh bread filled the hallway every morning at six.

core.definition: The act or process of using your nose to detect odors.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced ing with a short i. Say SMEL-ing, not SMEL-eeng, and keep the l clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a process rather than a judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use smelling as a standalone noun in everyday talk; they more often use the verb in the -ing form, as in smelling the flowers. The compound smelling salts is still known, but people usually say smelling salts only in discussions of old remedies or sports medicine. In science writing, smelling refers to the general sense.

distinctions.note: Smell is the everyday noun or verb; smelling emphasizes the ongoing act or process.
Sniffing is a quick, deliberate act of drawing air through the nose; smelling is the general act of detecting odors.

examples.everyday: Stop smelling the milk; if it smells sour, just pour it out.
examples.professional: Smelling a sample before testing it is a quick check, but it does not replace the lab results.
examples.analytical: Smelling is often treated as the least rational of the senses, yet it shapes memory and emotion powerfully.

nuance.analogy: Like a scout sent ahead of your other senses, smelling gathers information before you notice it.
nuance.etymology: From the verb smell, from Old English smyllan, with the -ing ending.
common_mistakes: Using smelling as a noun for a particular smell; say smell, as in a nice smell.
Confusing smelling with smelly; smelling is the act, while smelly means having a bad smell.

senses.definition: One who smuggles things.
senses.example: The smuggler hid bags of contraband in a false bottom beneath the truck bed.

senses.definition: A vessel employed in smuggling.
senses.example: The old schooner, a notorious smuggler, slipped past the revenue cutter in the fog.

core.definition: A person who secretly brings goods into or out of a country illegally, usually to avoid taxes or bans.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SMUG. The ending -ler is a weak syllable with the American r-colored vowel, so it sounds like ler, not lore. Say the gg as one g sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral. It implies breaking the law, though in stories about history or adventure it can be romantic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use smuggler for people who bring drugs, weapons, cigarettes, or other banned or taxed goods across borders. People talk about drug smugglers in the news and about smugglers in historical movies and novels. It is a normal, neutral word in conversation and news, and the verb is smuggle.

distinctions.note: A trafficker usually moves people or illegal goods in large commercial networks, while a smuggler is a more general term for anyone moving goods secretly across a border.
A bootlegger specifically makes or sells illegal alcohol, especially during Prohibition, while a smuggler can carry any illegal or untaxed goods.

examples.everyday: The news said the police caught a smuggler at the border with a car full of cigarettes.
examples.professional: Our security team traced the smuggler's shipments through three shell companies.
examples.analytical: Historians often portray the eighteenth-century smuggler as a folk hero, though his trade depended on bribery and fraud.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that runs underground, carrying goods past the checkpoints where everyone else must stop.
nuance.etymology: From Low German smuggeln, related to Dutch smokkelen, meaning to smuggle.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the gg as two separate g sounds, as in SMUG-gler.
Using smuggler for a legal importer or a business that is just unusual.

senses.definition: Contemptful, mocking.
senses.example: He made a sneering comment about their closeness.

senses.definition: The act of one who sneers.
senses.example: Her sneering at my cheap sweater made me wish I had stayed home tonight.

core.definition: Showing contempt or scorn, usually through a mocking tone or facial expression.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SNEER-ing. The second syllable is a reduced vowel followed by ng, so do not add an extra syllable like 'sneer-ee-ing'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, implying contempt and disrespect toward the target.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sneering to describe a tone of voice, a smile, or a remark that shows contempt. It is common in news, reviews, and everyday talk about people who look down on others. Calling someone's remark sneering is a direct criticism, so use it carefully in workplaces.

distinctions.note: Mocking can be playful or teasing, while sneering always shows real contempt.
Scornful is more general and a little more formal, while sneering stresses a visible or audible expression of contempt.
Derisive is more formal and literary, and it focuses on ridicule rather than the facial or vocal expression.

examples.everyday: Don't give me that sneering look; I'm only trying to help.
examples.professional: His sneering comments in the review meeting made people stop offering ideas.
examples.analytical: The sneering tone of the essay undermines its argument by letting contempt stand in for reasons.

nuance.analogy: A sneering tone is like a cold draft under a door: you feel it before anyone says it outright.
nuance.etymology: Present participle form of the verb sneer.
common_mistakes: Using sneering for mild disagreement; it implies real contempt.
Saying 'sneering at' with a noun object without a prepositional phrase, such as 'a sneering person' instead of 'a person who sneers'.

senses.definition: American and Oxford British English standard spelling of sodomize.

core.definition: To force another person into anal sex, or to commit anal sex on another person. In legal use it describes a sexual assault.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SAH-, and reduce the second vowel to a schwa. The American vowel in the first syllable is the open sound of 'father', not the 'saw' sound of British English.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. The word describes a violent or non-consensual act in most legal and public use, and it can be offensive or distressing in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: This verb appears mainly in legal texts, court reports, news about criminal cases, and academic discussion. Americans usually prefer terms like sexual assault or rape in everyday speech and in the news. Using sodomize in casual conversation would sound stiff, unusual, and disturbing, so reserve it for formal or legal contexts.

examples.everyday: I read in the news that the man was charged with sodomizing a child, and I still can't believe it.
examples.professional: The bill defines the offense as sodomizing another person without that person's consent.
examples.analytical: Legal scholars argue that the verb sodomize blurs the difference between consensual conduct and violent assault.

nuance.analogy: Sodomize is like a heavy legal sledgehammer: it hits hard and clearly, so it belongs only in courtrooms and formal records, not in casual talk.
nuance.etymology: From sodomy plus the verb-forming suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as in 'saw' (SAW-duh-mize), which is a British pattern.
Using it casually or as a joke, which sounds offensive and inappropriate in American English.

senses.definition: An upholstered seat with a raised back and one or two raised ends, long enough to comfortably accommodate two or more people.
senses.example: He bought a big sofa two days before his relatives arrived.

senses.definition: (historical) A slave soldier who served in the army of the Mali Empire.
senses.example: In the fourteenth century, the sofa served the emperor as a trusted soldier and bodyguard.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To furnish with one or more sofas.
senses.example: The designer sofaed the hotel lobby with plush blue seating before the grand opening.

senses.definition: To seat or lay down on a sofa.
senses.example: Exhausted after the shift, she sofaed by the window with a cup of tea.

core.definition: A long upholstered seat with a back and arms, big enough for two or more people to sit on comfortably.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SOH-, and make the final vowel a soft schwa, 'fuh', not 'fah'. Americans say the second syllable quickly, and it is not the Spanish 'sofá' with stress on the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word about furniture and carries no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, many people say couch instead of sofa, especially in casual talk. Sofa sounds a bit more formal or is used in furniture stores, interior design, and real estate listings. You can use either word in the home without sounding odd, and both are understood everywhere.

distinctions.note: Couch is the everyday American word and is more casual. Sofa sounds slightly more formal and is common in stores and written descriptions.
A loveseat is a smaller seat for two people. A sofa is longer and seats three or more.

examples.everyday: We spent the whole Sunday watching movies on the sofa.
examples.professional: The furniture catalog lists the sofa in three colors, and delivery takes about two weeks.
examples.analytical: The sofa in the parlor was a symbol of middle-class comfort and the new domestic ideals of the nineteenth century.

nuance.analogy: A sofa is like a bench that grew a back and arms and invited you to stay awhile.
nuance.etymology: From Arabic suffa, a bench or raised platform, which reached English through Turkish and French.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (suh-FOH) as in Spanish sofá.
Saying sofa when speaking casually to Americans, where couch is more common in everyday talk.

sofa.etymology: Borrowed from French *sofa*, ultimately from Arabic *صُفَّة* (“a long seat made of stone or brick, covered with rich carpets and cushions and used for sitting”).

senses.definition: The beliefs or doctrines of the solifidians.

core.definition: The theological belief that sinners are justified before God by faith alone, apart from works of the law, as taught by Protestant reformers.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'FID' in the third syllable, and the endings 'ee-uh-niz-um' are weak. Many learners stress the first syllable instead, so keep the stress on the middle of the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarship, but often polemical when used by critics. Catholic writers sometimes use it to label a view they reject, so the word can sound like an accusation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet 'solifidianism' in theological writing, debates about justification, and church history. Protestants usually prefer the phrase 'justification by faith alone' or 'sola fide,' while critics use 'solifidianism' to describe a view they think separates faith from works. In everyday conversation, most people would say 'justification by faith' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Justification by faith' is the standard name used by the teaching itself; 'solifidianism' is a broader, more abstract label, often used by outsiders.
Antinomianism rejects the moral law entirely, while solifidianism is about how a person is justified, not whether moral obedience matters.

examples.everyday: My Catholic friend said Protestants are too focused on faith and not enough on good works, which she called solifidianism.
examples.professional: In the seminar, we defined solifidianism carefully so students would not confuse the doctrine with antinomianism.
examples.analytical: The critics of solifidianism argue that separating justification from sanctification risks reducing faith to a mere intellectual assent.

nuance.analogy: Like a ticket that admits you to the stadium: faith gets you in the door, while good works show that you belong in the seats you were given.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'sola fide' (by faith alone), with the suffix '-ism' for a doctrine; 'sola' is from 'solus' (alone) and 'fide' is the ablative of 'fides' (faith).
common_mistakes: Using 'solifidianism' as a neutral term in front of a Protestant audience, where it may sound like an insult.
Confusing 'solifidian' (a person who holds the doctrine) with 'solidarian' or other similar-sounding words.
nuance.biblical_note: The doctrine rests on the Greek word 'pistis' (faith, trust) and the Greek phrase 'dikaioō' (to justify, to declare righteous). Romans 3:28 says a person is justified by faith apart from works of law. Romans 4:5 describes God justifying the ungodly who believe. Ephesians 2:8-9 says salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one may boast.

traditions.view: Orthodox Christians affirm that faith is necessary for salvation but insist that faith is expressed in love, obedience and the sacraments, and see justification as a lifelong process of transformation, or theosis. They generally reject the idea that faith alone is the full account of salvation.

Catholics teach that justification is a gift of grace that begins with faith but also includes charity, baptism and cooperation with grace, so that good works contribute to a person's growing righteousness. The Council of Trent condemned the view that faith alone justifies.

Most Protestants, including Lutherans and Reformed Christians, affirm justification by faith alone (sola fide), with good works following as the fruit of faith. Anglicans and Baptists largely agree, though they differ in how they relate faith, baptism and works.

senses.definition: In a sorrowful manner; with sorrow and regret.

core.definition: In a sad, regretful way, showing sorrow through how you speak, look, or act.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SOR. The final -ful is reduced to a quick 'fuh', and the ending is a clear 'lee', not 'lee-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes sadness in a way that often sounds dignified or literary rather than dramatic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing, storytelling, or formal speech, not in casual chat. You might hear it in a eulogy, a news report, or a novel. In conversation, people usually say 'sadly' or 'with a sad look' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Sadly' is far more common in everyday speech and can introduce a sad fact ('Sadly, the store closed'). 'Sorrowfully' describes how someone behaves or looks while feeling sorrow.
'Regretfully' focuses on a sense of having made a mistake or missed a chance. 'Sorrowfully' focuses on deep grief or sadness.

examples.everyday: She shook her head sorrowfully when she heard that her old neighbor had moved away.
examples.professional: The director sorrowfully announced that the project would be canceled after three years of work.
examples.analytical: The poet speaks sorrowfully of exile, yet he never abandons the hope that the community will return.

nuance.analogy: Like a gray sky that stays gray all day, sorrowfully describes sadness that hangs over an action.
nuance.etymology: From 'sorrowful' plus the adverb ending '-ly'; 'sorrow' comes from Old English 'sorh'.
common_mistakes: Using it in casual speech where 'sadly' or 'with a sad face' is more natural.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable (soh-ROW-fuh-lee) instead of the first.

senses.definition: Apologizing for speaking without your microphone on.

core.definition: An apology you say when you realize your microphone was off during a call or video meeting, so others could not hear you.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MUTE, the last word. Was is weak here, so it sounds like 'wuz'. Keep the r in sorry and say on quickly, since it is unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly. It is a light, self-deprecating apology that people accept easily.
nuance.usage_note: This is a very common line in Zoom, Teams and Google Meet calls in American workplaces, and it is often said with a laugh. A natural reply is 'No worries, happens to everyone' or 'Can you hear me now?' Use it right away, before you continue speaking, so the meeting moves on.

distinctions.note: Both are common; 'I was on mute' is the more idiomatic American phrase in video calls.
Being late concerns arrival time, while being on mute concerns audio during a meeting that has already started.

collocations: Sorry, I was on mute earlier

examples.everyday: Sorry, I was on mute. Could you say the dinner plan again?
examples.professional: Sorry, I was on mute during the budget update. My main point was that we need two more weeks.
examples.analytical: Sorry, I was on mute, so my objection to the sampling method was not heard; I will restate it now.

nuance.analogy: Like talking into a closed window: your words are there, but no one outside can hear them.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I was in mute' instead of 'on mute'.
Stressing the first word of mute as a noun-style stress; the stress on MUTE is the usual American pattern.

conversation.text: Sorry, I was on mute. What I said was, the report is done.
Oops, sorry, I was on mute the whole time.
"We can't hear you, Mike." "Sorry, I was on mute."

senses.definition: Highly skilled in, or specifically adapted to, a specific field.
senses.example: The hospital hired a specialized surgeon to repair the rare heart defect.

core.definition: Designed for, trained in, or requiring a particular field, skill, or purpose, rather than for general use.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'ci' is pronounced 'sh'. The final '-d' sound is a quiet, unvoiced ending on 'lyzd', so do not add an extra vowel after the z.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it suggests expertise, precision, or suitability for a specific task, but it can imply limited flexibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'specialized' for equipment, training, skills, and services, as in 'specialized software' or 'a specialized doctor.' It is common in everyday and professional speech. Americans often say 'a specialized tool for that' rather than 'a special tool for that' when they mean built for one purpose.

distinctions.note: Special means unusual or unique, while specialized means designed or trained for a specific field or purpose.
Specific means precisely defined or particular, while specialized means built for a particular field or expertise.

examples.everyday: You'll need specialized shoes if you want to go rock climbing, not just running shoes.
examples.professional: The migration requires specialized database expertise, so we should bring in a consultant.
examples.analytical: A specialized vocabulary can clarify a debate, but it can also exclude people who have not been trained in its terms.

nuance.analogy: Specialized is like a socket wrench compared with a multi-tool: it does one job particularly well because it was built for that job.
nuance.etymology: From specialize plus the past-participle suffix -ed.
common_mistakes: Using 'special' where 'specialized' is needed, as in 'special equipment' for technical tools.
Mispronouncing the 'ize' as 'eyes' or 'eyez' rather than 'lyzd'.
Adding a vowel after the final 'z' sound, which makes the word sound like an extra syllable.

senses.definition: In a specific manner, applying to or naming a particular thing or things, expressly, explicitly.
For a specific purpose or reason.
senses.example: The workshop was designed specifically for beginners who had never coded before.

core.definition: Expressly or explicitly; in a way that names one particular thing rather than a general category.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable. The 'ci' is 'f' followed by a short 'ik,' and the ending is a quick 'lee' with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It signals clarity and emphasis, and can sound a bit stiff when overused.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'specifically' to emphasize a point, as in 'I specifically asked for no cheese.' It often carries a mild note of insistence. Don't confuse it with 'especially,' which means 'to a great degree.' Americans also use 'specifically' in a softening way, such as 'I'm not specifically worried about that.'

distinctions.note: 'Specifically' means explicitly or in particular; 'especially' means to a higher degree or above all.

examples.everyday: I specifically told the cashier I wanted my coffee without sugar.
examples.professional: The tool was specifically designed for the sales team, so other departments may not need it.
examples.analytical: The author specifically rejects the claim that moral worth is inherited from one's group.

nuance.analogy: Like a pointing finger rather than a wave, it names one exact target.
nuance.etymology: From 'specific' plus the adverb suffix '-ly.'
common_mistakes: Using it in place of 'especially' when you mean 'to a great degree'
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'spe-SIF-ic-ly'

senses.definition: The Christian concept of fighting against the work of preternatural evil forces, based on the biblical belief in demons or evil spirits.
senses.example: Our pastor preached that prayer is a weapon in spiritual warfare against temptation.

core.definition: The Christian belief that believers must resist demonic and other evil spiritual forces through prayer, faith and Scripture.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress falls on WAR, with spir- as a secondary stress. Pronounce the final 'fare' as a reduced 'fair' sound, and link 'spiritual' smoothly into 'warfare'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral within religious settings; it can sound dramatic or alarming to outsiders, and it is sometimes used humorously for a hard day.
nuance.usage_note: Evangelical and charismatic Americans use this phrase often in prayer and preaching, as in 'We need to pray through this spiritual warfare.' Catholics and Orthodox Christians speak more of temptation and the spiritual struggle, and use the phrase less often. Outside church settings it can sound theatrical, so use it with people who share that language.

distinctions.note: The two are often used interchangeably, but warfare suggests a sustained, strategic struggle rather than a single fight.
Temptation is a personal pull toward sin; spiritual warfare is a broader struggle against evil forces, which many traditions understand as including demons.
Disciplines such as prayer and fasting are ongoing practices; spiritual warfare names the conflict those practices are meant to address.

examples.everyday: Some days my whole week feels like spiritual warfare, so I pray before I open my email.
examples.professional: In the staff meeting, the pastor said our outreach plan faces real spiritual warfare, so we should pray before we start.
examples.analytical: Paul's image of the armor of God in Ephesians 6 has long been read as a description of spiritual warfare, a struggle against forces beyond flesh and blood.

nuance.analogy: Spiritual warfare is like an unseen conflict behind the scenes of a city: you cannot see the fighting, but it shapes what happens on every street.
nuance.etymology: Spiritual is from Latin spiritualis; warfare is a compound of war and fare (journey or going), from Middle English.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on spir- instead of WAR; WAR carries the strongest stress.
Using spiritual war as a fixed phrase; the standard noun is warfare.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek phrase in Ephesians 6:12 refers to spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Ephesians 6:10-18 describes the armor of God that believers take up against the devil's schemes. Ephesians 6:12 says the struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers and powers. In 2 Corinthians 10:3-5 Paul says that though he lives in the flesh, his warfare does not follow fleshly methods, and his weapons are powerful for demolishing strongholds.

traditions.view: The Church teaches that the devil and demons are real and that Christians resist them through prayer and the sacraments; exorcism is performed only under formal approval by the Church.
The Orthodox speak of the spiritual struggle, an ascetic battle against passions and evil powers through prayer, fasting and confession, guided by a spiritual father.

Charismatic and Pentecostal Protestants often practice deliverance prayer and see active warfare against demons, while many Reformed and mainline Protestants emphasize moral struggle against sin with less focus on demonic encounters.

senses.definition: A play on words on a phrase in which the initial (usually consonantal) sounds of two or more of the main words are transposed.
senses.example: He accidentally said 'blushing crow' instead of 'crushing blow,' a classic spoonerism that made the room laugh.

core.definition: A playful slip or joke in which the first sounds of two or more words are swapped, like 'blushing crow' for 'crushing blow'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SPOO, with a lighter secondary stress on -ism's neighbor, -ZUM. The middle syllables are reduced to a quick 'uh' and 'rih'; the final r in 'Spooner' is pronounced because American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, sometimes humorous
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spoonerism mainly when talking about language, wordplay, or a funny mix-up in speech. It is named after the Oxford clergyman William Archibald Spooner, who was famous for such slips. A person who makes one has 'made a spoonerism,' and people often just say 'that was a spoonerism' when laughing at one.

distinctions.note: A spoonerism swaps sounds within phrases, while a malapropism replaces a word with a similar-sounding but wrong word, like 'epitaph' for 'epithet'.
A slip of the tongue is any speech error; a spoonerism is one specific kind in which initial sounds trade places.

examples.everyday: My friend said 'You have hissed all my mystery lectures,' which is a spoonerism of 'You have missed all my history lectures.'
examples.professional: In the linguistics workshop, the speaker used a spoonerism to show how the brain swaps sound units during speech planning.
examples.analytical: The spoonerism reveals that phonological units, not whole words, are often the level at which speech errors occur.

nuance.analogy: Like two people accidentally trading their shoes in a hurry, the sounds trade places.
nuance.etymology: Named after Rev. William Archibald Spooner (1844–1930), a warden of New College, Oxford, who was known for such slips.
common_mistakes: Saying 'spoon-er-ism' with equal stress on each syllable; the stress is on the first syllable.
Using spoonerism for any mistake in speech, when it means only a swap of initial sounds.

spoonerism.etymology: From *Spooner* + *ism*, who is supposed to have habitually made such slip-ups.

senses.definition: Any of various large coniferous evergreen trees or shrubs from the genus Picea, found in northern temperate and boreal regions; originally and more fully spruce fir.
senses.example: We planted a row of blue spruce along the north edge of the property.

senses.definition: The wood of a spruce.
senses.example: The guitar's soundboard is made from Sitka spruce for a bright, clear tone.

senses.definition: Made of the wood of the spruce.
senses.example: That spruce table is beautiful!

senses.definition: Smart, trim, and elegant in appearance; fastidious (said of a person).
senses.example: My grandfather always looked spruce in his pressed suit, even on fishing trips.

senses.definition: To arrange neatly; tidy up.
senses.example: Before the guests arrived, she spruced up the living room and set out fresh flowers.

senses.definition: To make oneself spruce (neat and elegant in appearance).
senses.example: He spruced himself up for the job interview with a fresh haircut and ironed shirt.

senses.definition: To tease. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: Stop sprucing me about my accent, Jake; it's getting old.

core.definition: To make something, or oneself, look neater and more attractive, often by cleaning or decorating.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long 'oo' sound, like 'loose', and the final e is silent. Don't use a short 'u' as in 'sprus' or pronounce an 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests making something look fresh, tidy and appealing.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, spruce is most often used in the phrasal verb 'spruce up', as in 'spruce up the yard before guests come'. As a verb without up, it sounds more literary. The tree sense is also common in the US, especially around Christmas, as in 'a spruce tree'.

distinctions.note: Tidy up means removing clutter or mess; spruce up adds the idea of making something look more attractive or stylish.
Freshen up can mean making oneself clean and refreshed; spruce up usually suggests improving appearance more visibly.

examples.everyday: Let's spruce up the living room before my parents visit.
examples.professional: We're going to spruce up the onboarding slides before the investor meeting.
examples.analytical: Editing that merely spruces up the prose can make a flawed argument look more finished without making it more sound.

nuance.analogy: Like giving an old car a fresh coat of wax, spruce up makes something look ready for guests.
nuance.etymology: The tree name may come from Middle English Pruce, meaning Prussia; the origin of the adjective spruce is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing spruce with a short 'u' as in 'sprus' or a long 'ee' sound, rather than 'sproos'.
Using spruce alone as a casual verb; in everyday speech, say 'spruce up'.

spruce.etymology: From Middle English *Spruce*, an alteration of *Pruce* (“Prussia”), from Medieval Latin, from a language, probably; for more, see Prussia.

senses.definition: Touchwood; tinder.
Synonym of taper, a thin stick used for transferring flames, especially a sulfur match.
Synonym of match, a thin chemically-treated stick used for creating flames.
Courage; spirit; mettle; determination.
To ejaculate.
senses.example: He spunked into the condom.

senses.definition: To waste (money etc.).

core.definition: Courage, determination, and lively spirit that help someone face a challenge or stand up for themselves.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the only syllable. The final nk is a nasal ng sound followed by a k; do not add a separate g or a vowel after the n.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises spirit and courage, especially in a young or small person who shows boldness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spunk in casual talk about kids, pets, or underdogs who show gutsy energy, such as 'That kid has spunk.' The verb sense (to ejaculate) and the sense of tinder are vulgar or obsolete in everyday use, so avoid the verb entirely. A natural reply is 'She sure does, I love that about her.'

distinctions.note: Courage is a general and serious word for facing danger or fear, while spunk is informal and suggests lively, feisty determination.
Grit emphasizes persistence through long hardship, whereas spunk is more about bold, lively spirit in the moment.

examples.everyday: That little kid has a lot of spunk, standing up to the coach like that.
examples.professional: The new hire showed real spunk by proposing a different approach in front of the executive team.
examples.analytical: Aristotle would say that spunk alone is not courage, since spunk can be impulsive and may lack good judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a small spark that starts a fire: little in size, but full of energy that can get things moving.
nuance.etymology: From an older sense meaning tinder or a spark, so spirit is figuratively a spark.
common_mistakes: Using spunk in formal writing, where courage or determination is more appropriate.
Confusing spunk with spank or spunky with spiky when pronouncing the nk ending.

senses.definition: To stand erect, bristle, especially from fear.
senses.example: The horrifying tales he told made my hair stand on end.

senses.definition: To place on its end.
senses.example: Carefully stand the heavy wooden crate on end so it fits in the corner.

core.definition: Of hair or skin, to rise up and become stiff, usually from fear, shock, or excitement.

pronunciation.tip: 'On' is a weak, unstressed word that sounds like 'ahn' or 'un' in speech. Stress falls on END, and the vowel in 'end' is the short 'eh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to vivid. It describes a strong physical reaction to something scary, surprising, or intense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'That made my hair stand on end' after a scary movie, a near accident, or a thrilling performance. The idiom is informal and vivid. A natural reply is 'Yeah, that was intense,' or 'I know, I was gripping my seat.'

distinctions.note: 'Give someone the creeps' describes a feeling of unease or disgust, while 'make your hair stand on end' describes a stronger physical shock or fear.
'Send shivers down your spine' is a more literary and descriptive phrase, while 'make your hair stand on end' is more casual and common.

collocations: make your hair stand on end
make someone's hair stand on end
make the hair on your arms stand on end

examples.everyday: That horror movie had me screaming, and the scene in the basement made my hair stand on end.
examples.professional: That outage alert made the whole on-call team's hair stand on end, because we had no clear rollback plan.
examples.analytical: Burke's account of the sublime describes a terror that makes the body respond, as when the hair seems to stand on end, although the response is aesthetic rather than purely physical.

nuance.analogy: Like a cat's fur rising when it sees a dog, your hair reacts before your mind has fully decided what to feel.
nuance.etymology: From Old English standan (to stand) and ende (end), meaning to stand upright on its end.
common_mistakes: Saying 'stand up on end', which is not standard; the idiom is 'stand on end'.
Using the idiom for mild annoyance, when it describes stronger fear, shock, or excitement.

senses.definition: One who stands.

core.definition: A person or thing that stands; this general sense is rare, and Americans usually choose a more specific word.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the final -er is a weak, r-colored syllable. Do not stress the final syllable or pronounce the vowel as a long 'ay'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is rarely used, so it can sound unusual or old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use stander, since they choose specific words such as standee for a passenger or bystander for a person watching an event. You may meet it in older writing or in technical descriptions of objects that stand. It is best to recognize it rather than use it.

distinctions.note: Standee is the common word for a passenger on a bus or train, while stander is a general and rare term.
Bystander means a person who watches without taking part, while stander only describes someone who is standing.

examples.everyday: The bus was full, so a stander near the door held the rail the whole way.
examples.professional: A stander at the back of the hall could see the slides but not the whiteboard, so we moved the screen.
examples.analytical: The word stander is rarely used, yet it reminds us that the simple act of standing has no fixed social meaning.

nuance.analogy: A stander is like a lamp post: it simply stands in place, and its meaning depends on the place around it.
nuance.etymology: From stand, plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing stander with standard, which is a different word with a different meaning.
Using stander in everyday conversation when standee or bystander is more natural.

senses.definition: A point of view; a perspective.
senses.example: Bathing once a month may save time, but from a cleanliness standpoint, it's not effective.

core.definition: A particular way of looking at a situation, shaped by your position, interests, beliefs, or experience.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on STAND. Both syllables of 'point' stress lightly, and the vowel in 'point' is the diphthong 'oy' (ɔɪ). Do not add an extra syllable like 'stan-duh-point'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a viewpoint without judging whether it is right or wrong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'standpoint' frequently in meetings and academic writing, almost always with 'from a . . . standpoint': 'From a financial standpoint, we can't afford it.' In casual speech people often say 'point of view' or 'perspective' instead. It sounds slightly formal but not stiff, so it works well in business and academic settings.

distinctions.note: Perspective is broader and can mean a way of seeing or a judgment about how important something is.
Viewpoint is more personal and often refers to an opinion you hold, while standpoint emphasizes your position or circumstances.
Stance is a publicly stated position on an issue, or a physical posture, while standpoint is the way of looking at things.

examples.everyday: From my standpoint the trip is too expensive, but you might see it differently since you've wanted to go for years.
examples.professional: From a data quality standpoint, we should exclude the 2019 records before we retrain the model.
examples.analytical: From the standpoint of natural law, the moral claim rests on the nature of the human person rather than on consent.

nuance.analogy: Like standing on one side of a hill: the view changes completely when you walk around to the other side.
nuance.etymology: English compound of 'stand' and 'point'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in my standpoint' instead of 'from my standpoint', which is the usual American phrase.
Confusing it with 'stance', which usually means a public position on an issue rather than a way of seeing things.

senses.definition: Synonym of dewdrop (“the plant Dalibarda repens”).

core.definition: A small, low-growing North American woodland plant, Dalibarda repens, with white star-shaped flowers; also called dewdrop.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'VY' in 'violet', which has three syllables in American speech. The middle syllable is a quick 'uh', and the 'r' in 'star' should be clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a botanical name used in nature writing and plant guides.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans would not know this plant name, so it appears mainly in botany, field guides and nature writing. In casual speech, people would say 'dewdrop' or describe the flowers. It is not a true violet, even though the name suggests it.

distinctions.note: A violet is a plant in the genus Viola; a star violet is a different genus in the rose family.
Dewdrop is the common name for the same plant, used in everyday speech and gardening.

examples.everyday: We found a little star violet blooming under the pines during our hike.
examples.professional: The botanical survey recorded star violet in the northern transect, where the forest floor was shaded.
examples.analytical: Because the star violet belongs to the rose family rather than the violet genus, its name reflects a common-name tradition rather than a close relationship.

nuance.analogy: A star violet is like a cousin who shares your family name but grew up in a different house.
nuance.etymology: From 'star' for its star-shaped flowers and 'violet' from the common name of the plant, a name that does not reflect true relation.
common_mistakes: Assuming a star violet is a true violet in the genus Viola.
Stressing 'VI-o-let' with the stress on the middle syllable.

senses.definition: A woman who is a leader in national or international affairs.
senses.example: The retired senator became a respected stateswoman who advised presidents on foreign policy for decades.

senses.definition: A female political leader who promotes the public good or who is recognized for probity, leadership, or the qualities necessary to govern a state.
senses.example: Voters admired her as a true stateswoman who put the public good above party loyalty.

core.definition: A woman who is a respected political leader, praised for wisdom, integrity, and dedication to the public good.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. 'Woman' is pronounced 'WUHM-uhn' in American speech, with a short 'oo' vowel, not 'WAH-man'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it praises a woman leader for integrity and vision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stateswoman' to honor a respected female political leader, often an older one. Many people prefer 'statesperson' in formal writing as a gender-neutral term. Calling someone a 'politician' is more neutral and can be used without praise.

distinctions.note: Stateswoman is specifically female, while statesperson is gender-neutral and common in formal American writing.
A politician seeks or holds office, while a stateswoman is praised for serving the public good.

examples.everyday: My mom admires the former governor because she thinks she was a real stateswoman who never played games.
examples.professional: The board praised the former minister as a stateswoman whose advice shaped the company's policy on trade.
examples.analytical: Historians often ask whether a stateswoman's legacy depends on her gender or on the qualities of her judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a seasoned coach who plans for the whole season, not just the next game.
nuance.etymology: From 'states' (genitive of state) plus 'woman'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'woman' as 'WAH-man' instead of 'WUHM-uhn'.
Using 'stateswoman' as a casual word for any female politician; it is a term of praise.

senses.definition: A single item in a statistical study.
senses.example: Each statistic in the study came from a survey of nearly ten thousand households.

senses.definition: A quantity calculated from the data in a sample, which characterizes an important aspect in the sample (such as mean or standard deviation).
A person, or personal event, reduced to being an item of statistical information.
senses.example: By dying from an overdose, he became just another statistic.

senses.definition: To analyze or describe using statistics.
senses.example: She statistics the sales data each quarter to spot seasonal trends in customer behavior.

senses.definition: To cite or calculate statistics.
senses.example: The commentator statistics the game in every broadcast, citing numbers no one else has noticed.

senses.definition: To comprise (as statistics)
senses.example: The annual reports statistic nearly every category of hospital spending in the region.

core.definition: A number calculated from sample data, such as a mean or standard deviation, that summarizes some feature of the sample.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, TIS, and reduce the first syllable to a quick 'stuh'. Do not say STAT-is-tic; the -tic ends like 'tick'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a term, though calling a person a statistic can sound cold.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the statistic that forty percent never finish' for one figure, and use statistics for the whole field or a collection of figures. In statistics, a statistic is any value computed from a sample, which differs from a parameter of the whole population. Being called a statistic usually means being reduced to a number.

distinctions.note: Statistics is the field or a collection of numbers; a statistic is one computed value from a sample.
A parameter describes the whole population and is usually unknown; a statistic is computed from a sample to estimate it.

examples.everyday: Did you see that statistic about how many people never read past the first page?
examples.professional: The team's dashboard shows the median response time as the key statistic for the service.
examples.analytical: Any statistic computed from a sample is itself a random variable, so its value varies from sample to sample.

nuance.analogy: A statistic is a photograph of a crowd taken from one sample: it summarizes the people in view but is not the whole crowd.
nuance.etymology: From Neo-Latin statisticus, of the state, from Latin status; the modern sense comes from German Statistik.
common_mistakes: Using statistic when you mean the field; say statistics, which takes a singular verb
Stressing the first syllable, as in STAT-is-tik

senses.definition: A person’s condition, position or standing relative to that of others.
senses.example: Superstition is highly correlated with economic status.

senses.definition: Prestige or high standing.
senses.example: Winning the Nobel Prize gave her enormous status in the research community.

senses.definition: A situation or state of affairs.
senses.example: What's the status of the investigation?

senses.definition: The legal condition of a person or thing.
senses.example: He is a status Indian.

senses.definition: The state (of a Canadian First Nations person) of being registered under the Indian Act.
senses.example: He is a status Indian.

senses.definition: A function of some instant messaging applications, whereby a user may post a message that appears automatically to other users, if they attempt to make contact.
senses.example: I'm just about to update my status to "busy".

senses.definition: Short for status epilepticus or status asthmaticus.
senses.example: The patient was admitted to the ICU with status after a prolonged seizure.

core.definition: A person's or thing's rank, position, or standing compared with others, or the current state of a situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a weak 'us' with a reduced vowel, so do not add an extra syllable like 'statoose'. STAT-us, with a short a, is also common in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral by default; positive when it means prestige or high standing, and negative when it suggests snobbery or status anxiety.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use status in business, school, and social settings, as in What's the status of the project? or She has high status at the firm. In casual talk, status often refers to social position or prestige and can have a slight edge. Status update is a common everyday phrase for a brief report, and marital status appears on many forms.

distinctions.note: State often means a condition or a country; status focuses on rank or position relative to others, or formal standing.
Position is a job or place in an organization; status is the level of respect or rank that comes with it.
Rank is a formal, ordered level; status can be informal, social, or legal.

examples.everyday: What's the status of my package? Did it ship yet?
examples.professional: Can you send me a status update on the migration before the stand-up?
examples.analytical: Social status in a small town often depends more on long-standing family ties than on current wealth.

nuance.analogy: Status is like a seat in a theater: it shows where you sit relative to everyone else.
nuance.etymology: From Latin status, a standing or condition, from stare, to stand.
common_mistakes: Confusing status with statue or state; the plural is statuses, not statuses with a different vowel.
Using status for a personal feeling; say mood or state of mind instead.

senses.definition: To remain in a particular place, especially for a definite or short period of time; sojourn; abide.
senses.example: We stayed in Hawaii for a week. I can only stay for an hour.

senses.definition: To continue to have a particular quality.
senses.example: Wear gloves so your hands stay warm.

senses.definition: To prop; support; sustain; hold up; steady.
senses.example: Use a wooden beam to stay the sagging roof until the repairs are finished.

senses.definition: To support from sinking; to sustain with strength; to satisfy in part or for the time.
senses.example: A cup of soup helped stay my hunger until dinner.

senses.definition: To stop or delay something.
senses.example: The governor stayed the execution until the appeal could be heard.

senses.definition: To stop; detain; keep back; delay; hinder.
senses.example: The storm stayed our departure by three hours.

senses.definition: To restrain; withhold; check; stop.
